progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b01: homeostasis, tolerance range and set point; the five parts; negative feedback opposes a change and eases as the variable returns; the pancreas as both receptor and control centre for glucose, insulin as a hormone, liver and muscle cells as effectors (b01 scene 7 outline). From Year 11: cellular respiration uses glucose; hormones are chemical messengers carried in the blood to target cells with receptors; proteins in membranes carry substances across. Not assumed: glycogen, glucagon, islets, beta and alpha cells, glycogenesis, glycogenolysis, glucose transporters, mmol/L.
progression.startsWith: Trace the response to rising glucose. The video opens: Picture a big bowl of pasta.
progression.stopsAfter: separating glucose (blood sugar, fuel), glycogen (stored glucose in liver and muscle) and glucagon (a hormone); stating the usual fasting range (about 4 to 6 mmol/L) and the temporary rise after a meal; naming the islets' beta cells (detect a rise, release insulin) and alpha cells (detect a fall, release glucagon) as receptor and control centre; explaining insulin's effects (muscle and fat cells take up more glucose as transporters move into the membrane; liver and muscle build glycogen, glycogenesis) and the fall in insulin as glucose returns (to a low background level); explaining glucagon's effect (the liver splits glycogen and releases glucose, glycogenolysis) when glucose falls; explaining why two opposing hormones give control in both directions; identifying the effectors (liver, muscle and fat cells, not the pancreas) and reading a graph in which insulin rises after glucose.
progression.nextLesson: the same kind of loop for water: how the kidneys control the water in blood (route entry bio-m8-b04).

teaching.task: After a big pasta meal, glucose pours into your blood. Overnight you eat nothing for eight hours or more, yet your brain keeps using glucose. What brings blood glucose down after the meal, and what pushes it back up while you sleep?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why glucose enters cells faster (more transporters in the membrane; 4); why glucose falls and why insulin then falls (5); where overnight glucose comes from (liver glycogen split and released; 6) and why the liver, not muscle, does that (6); why two hormones beat one (7). Attention: a meal and a night's sleep the learner has lived (1), a three-word trap (2), the car analogy (7). Visual medium: one glucose strip with a moving marker across a day, two coloured loop rings, and matched cell pairs that show the store filling and emptying. Apply: construct the falling loop (10a), interpret a two-line graph (10c). Remember: "in" and "gone", and the B for beta line.
teaching.conversationalApproach: After a big pasta meal glucose pours into your blood, then you sleep eight hours or more without eating while your brain keeps using glucose, yet a breakfast blood test is back in range, so the question is what pulls glucose down after the meal and what pushes it back up overnight. Three similar words get plain meanings first (glucose the blood sugar, glycogen the store, glucagon the hormone), with the fasting range of about four to six millimoles per litre. The pancreas is both receptor and control centre because its islets hold beta cells that detect a rise and release insulin and alpha cells that detect a fall and release glucagon. Insulin makes muscle and fat cells move extra glucose transporters into their membranes and switches on glycogenesis in the liver, so glucose leaves the blood; as glucose falls the beta cells release less insulin, which is negative feedback. Overnight, glucagon acts mainly on the liver, switching on glycogenolysis so the liver releases glucose. Driving over hills shows why two hormones are needed, insulin as the brake and glucagon as the accelerator, with the limit that both are released at some level all the time. Two exam checks follow (the pancreas signals but the liver, muscle and fat cells act; on a graph the hormone follows the glucose), then the memory aid insulin lets glucose in, glucagon acts when glucose has gone, and beta cells bring it down, and two exam questions with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Picture a big bowl of pasta. Within an hour, glucose from that meal is pouring into your blood. Then you sleep for eight hours or more without eating, and your brain keeps using glucose all night. Yet a blood test at breakfast would usually show glucose back in its normal range. So what pulls glucose down after the meal, and what pushes it back up while you sleep?
teaching.understandingCheck: 10a is a construct item on the falling side (the route's stop and the dotpoint's first verb). 10c is an interpret item from a two-line graph (the second verb, and the 2020 Q31 trap). Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it. Feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): the answer, the key reasons, givens underlined in the card as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B8-IQ1-01 (p 56): "construct and interpret negative feedback loops that show homeostasis by using a range of sources, including but not limited to: (ACSBL101, ACSBL110, ACSBL111)" with the listed example "glucose" ("construct" is attempt 1, "interpret" is attempt 2; sources: a loop diagram, a trace graph, a written description, painted tissue). B8-IQ1-02 (p 56): "investigate the various mechanisms used by organisms to maintain their internal environment within tolerance limits, including:" with the listed example "internal coordination systems that allow homeostasis to be maintained, including hormones and neural pathways (ACSBL112, ACSBL113, ACSBL114)" (insulin and glucagon as hormonal coordination; scenes 3 to 7).

design.visualSystem: A glucose strip owns the top of the frame from scene 2: the coded `lineGraph` drawn wide and short, y axis "blood glucose (mmol/L)" 3 to 9, x axis a 24-hour clock from noon to noon, a pale band from 4 to 6 marked "usual fasting range", and a bright marker dot that moves along the trace to show where the story is (after the meal, overnight, breakfast). Below it, the working area holds one painted plate or one pair at a time with callouts. b01's loop ring returns in two colours: a teal ring for the rising side (built in scenes 4 and 5) and an amber ring for the falling side (scene 6), shown side by side in scenes 7 and 8. Abstract glucose molecules are small coded hexagons (abstract, not plates). People are never drawn: no body outline; the brain plate stands for "your brain"; the meal is a tray of pasta. At most three bright text items at once; earlier labels dim to grey.
